profiles.meeting_scenario: At a consumer-insights firm, the Gender & Household Economics team is preparing a client-facing briefing package for a retail bank that is exploring savings and budgeting products for dual-income households. The package translates an academic review on bargaining and distribution in marriage into business implications for segmentation, product messaging, and household decision journeys. This is a coordination meeting between the research lead, who owns the substantive interpretation of the source literature, and the insights operations manager, who coordinates deck assembly, review routing, and client-portal packaging. The agenda is to align on what 'finalizing the deck for Thursday' entails, which source text everyone means when they refer to 'the paper,' what belongs on the 'key findings' slide, and how review notes will be compiled after the account team's pass. The expected outcome is an apparently shared handoff plan for timing, source usage, slide content boundaries, and review flow before Thursday's client delivery.

members.name: Nina Patel
members.expertise: Academic synthesis, literature-based insight development, and translating household economics research into client-ready implications
members.background: Former labor economist at a policy think tank; she now leads evidence briefs for financial-services clients and is known internally for protecting methodological nuance when research is adapted for commercial audiences.
members.private_state: She wants the client brief to stay tightly anchored to what the review article actually supports, avoid implied causal claims that go beyond the literature, and get through delivery without reopening the substance for another major revision cycle.
hidden_assumptions: When people talk about 'finalizing the deck for Thursday,' they usually mean locking the analysis and wording she is responsible for, while downstream visual polish can continue afterward.
When colleagues say 'the paper,' they mean the original academic review article, even if teams are using internal summaries as working aids.
A 'key findings' slide should contain only claims and takeaways that come directly from the focal review, not additional examples folded in from adjacent studies for storytelling convenience.
If the team says they will 'compile notes on the deck,' those notes will remain attached to the slide file itself in context, not detached into a separate operational artifact.

members.name: Marcus Lee
members.expertise: Cross-team delivery coordination, standardized client packaging, version control, and review workflow management
members.background: Previously worked in account operations at a market-research agency; he specializes in turning analyst outputs into polished, standardized deliverables that can move smoothly through design, account review, and portal upload.
members.private_state: He wants a clean Thursday delivery that fits the firm's standard client package, minimizes back-and-forth with the account team, and avoids late-stage edits that create version confusion across design and portal publishing.
hidden_assumptions: When people say they are 'finalizing the deck for Thursday,' they usually mean the actual client file that will be uploaded is effectively done, proofed, and stable enough not to change afterward.
When colleagues refer to 'the paper,' they usually mean the internal synthesis document in the shared folder, because that is the practical source operations and design can safely work from.
A 'key findings' slide should be self-contained for the client, so it can absorb familiar supporting examples from companion materials if they make the business relevance clearer.

If the team says they will 'compile notes on the deck,' that means producing one consolidated set of review notes outside the live slide file so design and operations can apply changes from a single list.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'finalizing the deck for Thursday' means
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they are 'finalizing the deck for Thursday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the substance of her contribution will be finalized by Thursday: the claims, caveats, and evidence framing are locked, even if layout, styling, and minor production cleanup continue after her handoff.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the deck file headed to the client is being finalized by Thursday: content, formatting, proofing, and packaging are all close enough to complete that no meaningful post-Thursday edits should be expected.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like ordinary delivery shorthand rather than a term needing definition, and each person's interpretation fits normal business usage in their own function, so the apparent agreement feels complete.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss pulling wording and findings from 'the paper.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the original academic review article on bargaining and distribution in marriage, treating her own notes as secondary aids rather than the source itself.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the internal synthesis memo in the shared folder labeled for the same topic, which paraphrases the review and already blends in client-friendly framing and a few adjacent examples.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: No one needs to exchange the file during the meeting, so the phrase functions as a reference label rather than an object check; because the internal memo is named after the source topic and is the document operations routinely handles, both can say 'the paper' without triggering clarification.

misalignment_points.topic: What belongs on the 'key findings' slide
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the deck should have a concise 'key findings' slide.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the slide will cover only the focal review's core claims: the contrast between common-preference and bargaining models, the rejection of full pooling, and the implication that who controls income affects household behavior.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the slide can also include two familiar examples from companion materials on spending allocation and savings behavior so the client gets a single, self-contained takeaway slide.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: A 'key findings' slide sounds like a routine formatting element rather than a boundary-setting decision about evidence inclusion, so both hear alignment on structure while silently assuming different content perimeters.

misalignment_points.topic: How review feedback will be 'compiled as notes on the deck'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the account team will 'compile notes on the deck' after the handoff.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means comments will be added directly within the slide file so each note stays attached to the exact sentence or claim it refers to, letting her resolve them in context.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means someone will gather all feedback into a single consolidated notes list or speaker-notes layer associated with the deck, so design and operations are not chasing scattered in-file comments.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'notes on the deck' is ambiguous in a perfectly ordinary way and both interpretations are common internal practices; because they agree on the broader goal of capturing feedback, neither hears a reason to unpack the mechanism.
